name: InfluxDB 3 Core
summary: A time-series database that validates writes into memory, persists a write-ahead log to object storage, exposes recent data through a queryable buffer, and materializes durable Parquet files with database retention semantics.

features.name: Timestamp and tag-set time-series identity
features.description: InfluxDB 3 Core organizes points into databases and tables with tags, fields, and timestamps; a row primary key combines the timestamp and tag set, while data is ordered by time.
benefits: Makes temporal identity and dimensions explicit for time-series queries
Separates identifying tags from measured field values
costs: Tag-set and schema choices influence sort and query costs
Wide or sparse tables increase ingestion and query resource use

features.name: WAL, queryable buffer, and Parquet pipeline
features.description: Validated writes enter an in-memory buffer, are flushed to a WAL for durability, become queryable in a recent-data buffer, and are periodically persisted to Parquet in object storage; recent Parquet data is cached.
benefits: Separates fast recent-query access from durable columnar persistence
Provides an explicit recovery boundary through WAL persistence
costs: Flush and persistence intervals trade durability, memory, and I/O overhead
Object storage and conversion work affect query freshness and resource usage

features.name: Query-time retention enforcement
features.description: InfluxDB 3 Core applies database retention periods when evaluating queries; expired points may remain physically stored until the retention service deletes them.
benefits: Provides a bounded logical observation window for applications
Decouples query visibility from immediate physical deletion
costs: Logical expiry and physical cleanup can be temporarily different
Retention is immutable after database creation in Core

mathematical_views.question: How do timestamps, tag sets, fields, and table schemas define a temporal relation whose rows remain ordered and queryable?
assumptions: A row is identified by its timestamp and non-null tag set
Table columns and data types are stable for the modeled schema
The view abstracts SQL and object-storage query execution

mathematical_views.question: When does a write transition from accepted memory state to WAL durability, query visibility, and Parquet persistence?
assumptions: The configured sync and flush policy defines the durability boundary
The queryable buffer merges recent and persisted representations
Parquet persistence preserves the modeled query observations

mathematical_views.question: How does a time-dependent retention predicate transform physically present points into the logical query-visible dataset?
assumptions: Retention is evaluated relative to the query-time notion of now
Physical deletion may lag logical filtering
The view does not equate query invisibility with immediate reclamation

benefits: Natural temporal filtering and dimensional querying
costs: Tag, field, and column-shape choices determine resource usage

benefits: Durable ingestion plus efficient long-term columnar storage
costs: Memory, object storage, and periodic persistence add operational tuning
Expired data can remain physically present and cleanup is asynchronous
